newsitem.title: UK: UK shares suffer biggest fall for two months.
newsitem.headline: UK shares suffer biggest fall for two months.

text.p: The UK's FTSE 100 index of leading shares suffered its biggest one-day decline in point terms for two months on Monday, as bank stocks tumbled and fears grew of a possible rise in British interest rates later this week.
Worries over the Labour government's first budget, confirmed for July 2, also helped send the index 58.5 points lower to 4,562.8 -- its biggest fall since a 65-point loss on April 1.

With Wall Street unsettled by fresh fears of a rise in U.S. interest rates, the FTSE 100 was in near free-fall at one stage late in the session, setting the scene for what analysts and traders said could be a jittery month.

The long-awaited market debut of banking group and former building society Halifax dominated trading activity, prompting profit-taking in other financial stocks as investment funds cashed in gains in the sector to finance the purchase of Halifax shares.

Halifax, valued among the top ten British companies after its storming market debut, closed at 735-1/2p -- well above the level expected just a few days ago -- in huge volume of over 647 million shares, about half the volume in the market as a whole.
Participants noted that other prospective financial flotations could absorb yet more of the cash held by fund management groups.

"The immediate outlook doesn't look so clever, with lots of supply around and with fears about the direction of fiscal and monetary policy," said Richard Kersley, UK investment strategist at BZW, investment banking arm of Barclays. Kersley pointed out that London was the only major European market to close lower, despite growing uncertainties over prospects for European monetary union (EMU) following the weekend poll victory for the French socialists.

With sterling seen as a safe haven amid the bout of EMU worries, there were fears of continued pressure on the overseas earnings of top companies which have already been squeezed by the currency's strength in recent months.
And with the Labour government's first budget confirmed for July 2, there were concerns over possible tax-raising measures targeted at companies and pension funds, making shares look vulnerable.
After reaching the latest of a succession of record highs towards the end of last month, dealers said the FTSE 100 could find if difficult to push higher in the short term.

"The merry-go-round has come to a halt for the time being...maybe the time between now and the end of the month is going to be a bit dull," said one senior dealer. The FTSE last week touched a near-record 4705.2.
UK shares found short-lived support from a rally in continental European markets and for a while the FTSE 100 looked reluctant to break decisively below the 4,600 level.

Yet an unsteady performance on Wall Street dragged shares lower towards the close, with the Dow down 25 points as London trading ended and the U.S. Treasury long bond down 4/32 points to yield 6.9 percent.
A stronger-than-expected U.S. purchasing managers' report helped drag U.S. markets lower, renewing fears about the risk of a rise in U.S. interest rates ahead of Friday's key U.S. employment report.

Bank stocks bore the brunt of the declines, as the Halifax flotation provided a cue for profit-taking in the sector which has been driven to record highs in recent months as investment funds pumped cash into proxies for the market debutante.
Barclays tumbled 53-1/2p to 11.33-1/2, Abbey National fell 32p to 848-1/2, Lloyds TSB Group shares lost 30-1/2p to 583-1/2 and National Westminster Bank Plc fell 21p to 723-1/2.
Worries about a hike in UK interest rates loomed as financial markets looked ahead to the debut meeting of the Bank of England's new monetary committee on Thursday and Friday.
